items.title: How Stanford Teaches AI Coding Now
items.summary: What does it take to build AI agents that deliver useful, reliable work? Stanford lecturer and Monaco Head of AI Mihail Eric joins Demetrios for a conversation inside a Waymo about how AI is changing software development - and what it takes to put agents into production. Mihail explains why he rebuilt most of his Modern Software Developer course, how he teaches students to avoid shipping AI slop, and why research, planning, and verification still matter as coding agents become more capable. They discuss Claude Code, agent loops, context engineering, memory and compaction, and how to design MCP tools around what an agent needs to accomplish. Then they go inside Monaco’s approach to sales agents, from turning meetings and emails into useful insights to building a custom agent harness. Along the way: lessons from Boris and Lee Robinson’s guest lectures, why company traces are becoming valuable assets, and Monaco’s unusual approach to brand building. What’s the biggest bottleneck in your agent workflows: context, tools, or verification? Let us know in the comments. items.title: 3 Ways an AI Agent Goes Rogue
items.summary: In episode 1040 of the SuperDataScience podcast, @JonKrohnLearns discusses with Amy Blackshaw, SVP at Palo Alto Networks, the three primary ways an AI agent can go rogue. Amy explains how agents can be subverted by malicious instructions, drift from their intended goals, or leak sensitive information through their reasoning processes. She shares real cases where an agent's own token was lifted and inherited everything it could touch.

items.title: Google's Suncatcher Prototype Runs Gemma 4 On A TPU In Orbit In A First AI Test
items.summary: Google Project Suncatcher successfully completed its first orbital test on October 1st, 2026, marking a shift in space computing. This mission explores how moving AI compute tasks to orbit can alleviate the increasing energy demand on terrestrial power grids. items.title: Why Consciousness Might Not Be Hard At All (Joscha Bach)
items.summary: Joscha Bach is a cognitive scientist and the founder of the California Institute for Machine Consciousness. SPONSOR: --- Parallel is a single platform for all your agentic research: web search built for AI agents, with Pareto-optimal quality, cost and speed. Get started: https://parallel.ai/mlst?utm_source=creator&utm_medium=podcast&utm_content=MLST --- Bach's null hypothesis is that consciousness is easy: an algorithm not much more complicated than the transformer, simple enough for an infant's brain to discover by itself. In this conversation with Tim, he lays out the Machine Consciousness Hypothesis in two parts. The first is that consciousness is a biological learning algorithm, the training algorithm that makes a brain like ours coherent. The second is that machines learning in self-organising ways might discover it in the same way. Either part can fail on its own. From there they ask why there will never be a Turing test for consciousness, why a chess program is already a zombie, and why faking a mind can sometimes be harder than building one. Bach's null hypothesis is that consciousness is easy: an algorithm not much more complicated than the transformer, simple enough for an infant's brain to discover by itself. In this conversation with Tim, he lays out the Machine Consciousness Hypothesis in two parts. The first is that consciousness is a biological learning algorithm, the training algorithm that makes a brain like ours coherent. The second is that machines learning in self-organising ways might discover it in the same way. Either part can fail on its own.

From there they ask why there will never be a Turing test for consciousness, why a chess program is already a zombie, and why faking a mind can sometimes be harder than building one.
